clinicalPearls: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive exocrinopathy affecting multiple epithelial tissues; the gene product CFTR is an apical anion (chloride and bicarbonate) channel that regulates the volume and composition of exocrine secretion (p.2245).

Major morbidity and mortality arise from pulmonary disease: copious hyperviscous adherent secretions obstruct small and medium airways, and a complex flora including Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is routinely cultured from CF sputum (p.2245).

P. aeruginosa shows stereotypic pathogenesis: an early sentinel colonization often becomes lifelong infection by the same strain, and over years evolves a mucoid (alginate-producing) phenotype that confers selective advantage and poor host prognosis (p.2245).
Radiographic sinusitis occurs in most patients with CF; the sinuses may act as a reservoir for bacterial seeding of the lower airways (p.2245).

Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causes chronic malabsorption, poor growth, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; high blood immunoreactive trypsinogen (used in newborn screening) and low fecal elastase-1 are characteristic (p.2245-2246).

CF-related diabetes mellitus occurs in >30% of adults and is multifactorial (endocrine pancreatic destruction plus, in some, insulin resistance); annual diabetes testing is recommended for adults with CF (p.2246, p.2248).
Men typically show complete involution of the vas deferens despite functioning spermatogenesis, and ~99% of males with CF are infertile (unable to conceive without in vitro fertilization) (p.2246).

Diagnosis is confirmed by disease-causing variants on both CFTR alleles and/or sweat chloride >=60 mEq/L together with characteristic exocrine manifestations; sweat electrolyte testing follows pilocarpine iontophoresis (p.2246-2247).

Several severe defects (F508del, G551D, nonsense alleles) predict pancreatic insufficiency, present in ~80% of patients; F508del alone accounts for ~85% of defective CFTR alleles in the United States (p.2247).

CFTR modulators (ivacaftor potentiator; lumacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor correctors) are highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT); triple combination therapy is projected to benefit >90% of patients and improves FEV1, reduces exacerbations, and lowers sweat chloride (p.2247-2248).

Pulmonary exacerbation poor-prognosis pathogens that are rigorously monitored include Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, and atypical mycobacteria; MRSA may also signal worse outcomes (p.2248).
Infection commonly persists despite modulator therapy, so chronic respiratory infection and inflammation continue even after substantial clinical improvement on HEMT (p.2248).
harrison.pathophysiology: Mutation of CFTR, an apical epithelial anion channel that conducts chloride and bicarbonate (~1480 amino acids, gated by ATP hydrolysis without active transport against gradient), impairs hydration and clearance of exocrine secretions. In the airway, loss of CFTR-dependent anion secretion depletes the periciliary fluid layer, causing ciliary collapse and failure to clear overlying mucus; mucoobstruction with chronic infection drives an aggressive, unrelenting neutrophilic inflammatory response with proteases and oxidants, leading to airway remodeling and bronchiectasis. Low airway-surface-fluid pH may impair bacterial killing. Similar mechanisms affect pancreatic acini/ducts (fibrotic destruction, cyst formation, exocrine and eventually endocrine insufficiency), hepatobiliary tissue (biliary obstruction, focal/multilobular cirrhosis, portal hypertension), and intestine (meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstructive syndrome). Over 2000 CFTR allelic variants are described and grouped into classes I-VI by molecular mechanism (e.g., F508del is a class II protein-maturation/folding defect degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum; G551D is a class III gating defect).
additionalDifferentials: Non-CF bronchiectasis (CF carrier status predisposes; heterozygous CFTR mutations implicated) (p.2247)
Chronic rhinosinusitis (associated with relative CFTR deficiency) (p.2247)
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens as an isolated forme fruste of CFTR mutation (p.2247)
Idiopathic/recurrent pancreatitis associated with CFTR mutation in at least one allele (p.2247)
additionalInvestigations: Sweat chloride after pilocarpine iontophoresis (chloride >=60 mEq/L supports diagnosis; highly specific) (p.2246-2247)
CFTR mutation analysis / panels of several hundred variants, or complete CFTR sequencing with splice-junction analysis (p.2246-2247)
Fecal elastase-1 (low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency) (p.2246)
Sputum culture surveillance for resistant pathogens (Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, atypical mycobacteria, MRSA) (p.2248)
FEV1 (% predicted) for monitoring and transplant referral thresholds (p.2248)
Annual diabetes mellitus testing in adults; monitor liver function and CYP3A drug interactions on modulator therapy (p.2248)
redFlags: Sputum culture growing Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, or atypical mycobacteria (poor prognostic indicators) (p.2248)
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (~5% of patients) suggested by failure to respond to aggressive inpatient antibiotics (p.2248)
FEV1 <30% predicted (threshold for lung transplant referral) (p.2248)
harrison.prognosis: Modulator and other therapies have transformed CF from a disease that historically led to death in early childhood to one with frequent survival well into the fifth decade and beyond; US median survival now exceeds 60 years. Genotype is of limited value for predicting respiratory rate of decline or longevity. End-stage pulmonary failure may be treated with lung transplantation (median survival >9 years among adults). Marked geographic disparity exists: median survival is <30 years in much of Latin America versus >60 years in the United States (p.2248-2249).
pitfalls: Hyperviscosity of eccrine sweat is NOT a feature of CF; the sweat test reflects defective ductal chloride reabsorption, not thick sweat (p.2247).
Anion flux through CFTR does NOT involve active transport against a concentration gradient (p.2245-2246).
Genotype does NOT reliably predict respiratory prognosis or longevity, even though some severe alleles predict pancreatic insufficiency (p.2247).
A subset of patients with F508del respond poorly to triple combination therapy, so modulator benefit is not universal (p.2248).
HEMT may reduce sputum bacterial density but does NOT eradicate infection; chronic respiratory infection and inflammation persist (p.2248).

CF has been underdiagnosed outside historically white populations (Eastern Europe, Latin America, Asia, India, and US minorities), often due to rare/poorly characterized variants and limited access to DNA/sweat testing (p.2249).
harrison.severityClassification: CFTR mutations are categorized by molecular mechanism into classes I-VI: class I, absent synthesis (e.g., nonsense mutations G542X, R553X, W1282X); class II, defective protein maturation and premature degradation (e.g., F508del, ~85% of US alleles, the most common); class III, disordered gating/regulation (e.g., G551D, ~4% of patients); class IV, defective conductance through the channel pore; class V, reduced transcript number from promoter/splicing abnormality; class VI, accelerated turnover from the cell surface. Severity is not formally graded by stage; FEV1 <30% predicted is used as a lung-transplant referral threshold (p.2246, p.2248).
